analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, military, federal-employee, and private insurance to cover medically necessary food and vitamins.
analysis.headline: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship but never received a committee vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from May 2017 until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Some people with rare digestive and inherited metabolic disorders cannot eat ordinary food and need doctor-prescribed, specially formulated products that can cost thousands of dollars a month. Today most health plans treat that food as groceries, not medicine, and refuse to pay for it, leaving families to bear the full cost or watch their children get sicker. This bill would require Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, military and federal-employee health plans, and private insurance to cover prescribed medical food and vitamins for these conditions, just as they cover drugs. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with inherited metabolic disorders, short bowel syndrome, severe food allergies, eosinophilic disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease who need medically necessary food, along with their families, who currently pay out of pocket for products that can run to many thousands of dollars a year. Children on Medicaid and CHIP would gain a guaranteed benefit, and the roughly nine million federal-employee households and military families covered by FEHBP and TRICARE would gain coverage too.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients with rare digestive and metabolic disorders

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would treat prescribed medical food as a covered item, paying 80% of a fee schedule amount the same way it pays for other medical supplies, and Medicare Part D drug plans would have to cover prescribed medically necessary vitamins [S3].
Medicaid and CHIP would be required to cover medically necessary food and vitamins as mandatory benefits, guaranteeing the service to low-income children in every state [S3].

TRICARE (military families), the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and all group and individual private health insurance would have to cover the same food and vitamins, with the private-insurance mandate applying to plan years starting a year after enactment [S3].

The bill narrows coverage to products prescribed for a defined list of diseases and expressly excludes weight-loss foods, foods marketed as gluten-free for celiac disease, and foods marketed for diabetes, aiming the mandate at patients whose doctors say ordinary diet modification is not enough [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government (Medicare at 80% of a set fee schedule, plus its share of Medicaid and CHIP), state Medicaid programs, and private health insurers, whose premiums or budgets would absorb the cost of the newly covered food. The bill's own findings acknowledge that the food is expensive; spreading that cost across taxpayers and premium payers is the trade-off for lifting it off affected families.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, state Medicaid budgets, and private insurers

drawbacks.text: It is a new mandatory spending and coverage requirement: Medicare would pay 80% of the cost of medical food, and Medicaid and CHIP coverage would be mandatory for states, so federal and state budgets would take on new, ongoing costs with no dedicated funding source in the bill [S3].

Private insurers would face a new benefit mandate that would raise premiums for all policyholders, spreading the cost of covering a small, very sick population across everyone who buys insurance [S3].

The exclusions are real gaps for patients: people whose medical need is gluten-free food for celiac disease or therapeutic diets for diabetes would get no new coverage even if their food is medically necessary and expensive [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the affected families the benefit is unambiguous: insurance would finally pay for food their doctors prescribe as medical treatment, and the bill's own findings warn that untreated patients risk hospitalization, impaired growth, and death. The costs are real but targeted — new federal and state spending and a modest premium impact — and the bill tries to control them by limiting coverage to prescribed products for a defined list of serious conditions and excluding everyday diet foods. The main honest criticism is that it adds mandatory entitlement spending without an offset, which is why in a normal process it would need a cost estimate and a funding decision before moving.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bob Casey (D-PA) introduced the bill on May 22, 2017 together with Senator Chuck Grassley (R-IA), giving it a Republican co-lead from the start [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid [S5].
Three senators cosponsored the bill — one Republican and two Democrats [S4] — but no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].
The Finance Committee held no markup, and the Senate never voted on the bill before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Families with these disorders remained responsible for the full cost of prescribed medical food, and health insurers and federal programs kept the savings from not covering it. The bill's bipartisan sponsors gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and federal programs; patients kept paying

sides.party_line_note: The bill was co-led by a Democrat (Casey) and a Republican (Grassley), and its three cosponsors split 1 Republican and 2 Democratic, so no party opposed it on the record — it simply never reached a vote [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill requires group and individual private plans, FEHBP carriers, and Medicare Part D and Advantage plans to cover prescribed medical food and vitamins — a new mandated benefit whose cost would otherwise stay with patients. Their financial interest in this bill runs directly against the families the bill is for.

industries.industry: Medical food and specialized nutrition manufacturers
industries.note: Companies that make amino-acid formulas, elemental infant formulas, and low-protein modified foods would gain a large, guaranteed reimbursed market under Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, FEHBP, and private insurance. Their gain comes from patients finally getting coverage for products doctors already prescribe, so it runs alongside patients' interests.

Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP would take on new mandatory spending — Medicare at 80% of a fee schedule for medical food — and states could not drop the Medicaid benefit. Taxpayers would absorb costs that currently fall on individual families.
